title: The Equator and the Poles
summary: How the equator, the line of zero latitude, and the North and South Poles, Earth's two most extreme points, mark opposite ends of our planet's climate.
poll: I would find it easier to live near the equator than near one of the poles.

versions.title: The Middle and the Ends
versions.text:
Earth has one line in the middle. We call it the equator.

Earth has two far ends too. We call each end a pole. One is up top. One is down low.

The sun beams straight down here. This direct heat lasts all year.

At the poles, the sun sits low. Its light spreads out. The poles get just a bit of heat.

So one spot stays hot all year. The other stays cold all year.

This has a name: climate. Climate is what a place gets most of the time.

Many live near the equator. Thick woods grow there too.

Few live at the poles. Ice and snow cover the ground there.

versions.title: The Equator and the Poles
versions.text:
Earth has one special line that circles the whole planet. We call it the equator.

Earth also has two extreme ends, one at the top and one at the bottom. We call each end a pole. This gives us the North Pole and the South Pole.

The sun shines almost straight down on the equator all year. This spot gets strong, direct heat nearly every day.

At the poles, sunlight comes in at a low angle. The light spreads out. The poles get only a small amount of heat.

Because of this, places near the equator stay hot all year. Places near the poles stay cold all year.

This long pattern of weather has a name. It is called climate. Climate tells us what weather to expect.

Many people live near the equator. Thick forests often grow easily in the warm, wet weather.

Very few people live at the poles. Thick ice and deep snow cover the ground there all year.

versions.title: The Equator and the Poles: Earth's Extremes
versions.text:
Earth has one special line that circles the planet exactly in the middle. We call it the equator.

Earth also has two extreme points, one at the top of the globe and one at the bottom. We call each point a pole, giving us the North Pole and the South Pole.

The sun's rays hit the equator almost perpendicularly all through the year. This gives that spot strong, direct heat nearly every day.

At the poles, sunlight arrives at a very low angle instead. The light spreads out over a wide area, so the poles get only a small amount of heat.

Because of this big difference, places near the equator stay hot and humid all year. Places near the poles stay cold for almost the entire year.

This long, seasonal pattern of weather is called climate. Climate tells us what weather to expect in a place, season after season.

Many people live near the equator, where thick vegetation, like green rainforests, often thrives in the warm, wet weather.

Very few people live right at either pole. A brief summer thaw may come, but thick ice and deep snow cover the ground for most of the year.

versions.title: The Equator and the Poles: Earth's Extremes
versions.text:
Earth has one special line that circles the planet exactly in the middle. We call it the equator.

Earth also has two extreme points, one at the top of the globe and one at the bottom. We call each point a pole, giving us the North Pole and the South Pole, both far from the equator.

The sun's rays hit the equator almost perpendicularly throughout the year. This gives that spot strong, direct heat nearly every day, with little change between seasons. The heat stays strong whether it is January or July.

At the poles, sunlight arrives at a very low angle instead. The light spreads out over a much wider area, so the poles get only a small fraction of the heat. Even in their short summer, the poles never feel truly warm.

Because of this big difference, places near the equator stay hot and humid all year, while places near the poles stay cold for almost the entire year.

This long, seasonal pattern of weather is called climate. Climate tells us what weather to expect in a place, season after season and year after year. It shapes how people live, farm, and dress.

Many people live near the equator, where thick vegetation, like green rainforests, often thrives in the warm, humid weather found there. Crops can often grow all year long in such a place.

Very few people live right at either pole. A brief summer thaw may come, but thick ice and deep snow cover the ground for most of the year, leaving the land mostly empty.

versions.title: The Equator and the Poles: Earth's Extremes
versions.text:

Earth also has two extreme points, one at the top of the globe and one at the bottom. We call each point a pole, giving us the North Pole and the South Pole, both as far from the equator as a place can be.

The sun's rays hit the equator almost perpendicularly throughout the entire year, with the sun passing nearly overhead at midday. This gives that spot strong, direct heat nearly every day, with little change between seasons.

At the poles, sunlight arrives at a very low angle instead, for much of the year. The light spreads out over a much wider area, so the poles get only a small fraction of the heat the equator gets.

Because of this huge difference, places near the equator stay hot and humid all year, while places near the poles stay bitterly cold for almost the entire year.

This long, seasonal pattern of weather is called climate. Climate tells us what kind of plants, animals, and people a region can support over time.

Many people live near the equator, where thick vegetation, like green rainforests, often thrives in the warm, humid weather found there.

Very few people live right at either pole. A brief summer thaw may come, but thick ice and deep snow cover the ground for most of the year, leaving little room for plants.

versions.title: The Equator and the Poles: Earth's Climate Extremes
versions.text:

Earth also has two extreme points, called the poles, one at the top of the globe and one at the bottom. The North Pole and the South Pole mark the extremity of each hemisphere, as far from the equator as any place on the planet can be.

The sun's rays strike the equator almost perpendicularly throughout the year, with the sun passing nearly overhead at midday regardless of season. This delivers intense, concentrated heat nearly every day, with little seasonal change. Day after day, the equator receives roughly the same strong dose of sunlight.

At the poles, sunlight strikes at a very low angle for much of the year, and this dispersion spreads the light's energy across a much wider area. As a result, the poles receive only a small fraction of the heat intensity the equator absorbs. Even during their short summer, the poles rarely feel truly warm.

Because of this huge difference, regions near the equator stay hot and humid all year, while regions near the poles stay bitterly cold for nearly the entire year, apart from a brief thaw.

This long, seasonal pattern of weather is called climate, and climate largely determines what a region can sustain, including its plants, animals, and people. It also shapes how people farm, build, and travel.

Very few people live permanently at either pole, since thick ice and deep snow blanket the ground most of the year, leaving little room for plants to take root or for farms to grow food.

versions.title: The Equator and the Poles: Earth's Climate Extremes
versions.text:
Earth has one defining imaginary line that circumscribes the entire planet exactly at its midpoint, situated precisely halfway between the uppermost and lowermost extremities, visible on virtually every globe and world map ever produced throughout recorded history. We call it the equator.

Earth also possesses two extreme points, called the poles, one located at the very top of the globe and one at the very bottom. The North Pole and the South Pole mark the extremity of each hemisphere, representing the maximum possible distance from the equator that any location on the planet could conceivably occupy, however remote or inaccessible.

The sun's rays strike the equator almost perpendicularly throughout the entire year, because the sun passes nearly directly overhead at midday irrespective of the particular season. This consistently direct sunlight delivers intense, concentrated heat nearly every day, with remarkably little seasonal variation, in stark contrast to regions situated considerably farther from the equator. Day after day, year after year, the equator receives roughly the same powerful dose of sunlight, with almost no meaningful change at all.

At the poles, by sharp contrast, sunlight strikes at an extremely oblique angle for the majority of the year, and this dispersion spreads the light's energy across a far wider expanse of ground than it ever would near the equator. Consequently, the poles receive only a small fraction of the heat intensity that the equator absorbs on a given day, even during their comparatively brief polar summer. Frost can return to the poles without much warning, even during their short, pale summer.

Because of this enormous disparity in solar intensity, regions near the equator remain hot and humid throughout the entire year, whereas regions near the poles remain dangerously, bitterly cold for nearly the entire year, aside from a brief summer thaw lasting merely a few weeks.

This long-term, consistent pattern of weather is known as climate, and climate largely dictates what a given region can realistically sustain, including its plants, animals, and human activities, shaping entire civilizations across generations. It also shapes how whole communities farm, construct dwellings, and travel across long distances.

Many people reside near the equator, where dense, verdant rainforests often flourish in the warm, humid conditions, sustaining an extraordinarily diverse array of life found almost nowhere else across the planet. Crops can often be cultivated there throughout the entire year without much difficulty or careful planning.

Very few people reside permanently at either pole, since thick ice sheets and deep snow blanket the terrain year-round, leaving almost no exposed soil anywhere for vegetation to establish roots and flourish, let alone for any agricultural activity to ever succeed.

At the poles, sunlight arrives at a far lower angle, spreading its energy over a wider area, which is why the poles stay extremely cold except for a brief seasonal thaw during their short summer.

keyWords.definition: one half of the Earth, divided by the equator or another great circle
keyWords.example: Australia lies in the Southern Hemisphere.

keyWords.definition: the strength or amount of something, such as heat or light
keyWords.example: The intensity of the midday sun made the pavement too hot to touch.

keyWords.definition: the spreading out of something over a wider area
keyWords.example: The dispersion of light through the window made the room glow softly.

keyWords.definition: to keep something going or support it over time
keyWords.example: A balanced diet helps sustain a person's energy throughout the day.

keyWords.definition: the furthest point or end of something
keyWords.example: The lighthouse stood at the extremity of the rocky peninsula.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Sunlight angle makes the equator and poles opposite climate extremes
Rainforests and ice sheets are essentially the same ecosystem
The poles receive more total sunlight each year than the equator
Only trained scientists are ever permitted to study the equator
questions.why: The article traces how sunlight angle creates the equator's intense heat versus the poles' cold, and how that climate shapes what each region can sustain.

wrong.B: Rainforests and ice sheets are described as dramatically different environments.
wrong.C: The article shows the poles receive far less heat, not more.
wrong.D: No restriction on who may study the equator is mentioned.

questions.stem: What happens at the extremity of each pole during the polar summer?
options: The pole there temporarily becomes a thriving rainforest
A brief thaw occurs, but the region stays bitterly cold overall
Temperatures there briefly exceed those found at the equator
The entire ice sheet there disappears permanently for good
questions.why: Near the poles, summer is short, and it stays cold for most of the year.

wrong.A: No transformation into a rainforest is described.
wrong.C: The poles receive far less heat than the equator throughout the year.
wrong.D: Thick ice sheets are described as persisting year-round.

questions.stem: What does the article identify as the cause of the equator's intense heat?
options: Human activity near the equator that traps extra heat
Ocean currents that warm the equator artificially each day
Sunlight striking it almost perpendicularly nearly every day
The equator being located physically closer to the sun
questions.why: The article attributes the equator's consistent heat to sunlight striking it almost perpendicularly throughout the year.

wrong.A: Human activity is not presented as a cause in the article.
wrong.B: Ocean currents are not discussed as the cause.
wrong.D: Distance from the sun does not meaningfully differ between the equator and poles.

questions.stem: In the article, the word intensity most nearly refers to —
options: the strength or amount of the sun's heat energy
the number of people who live in a given region
the particular color of the sky at different times
the distance measured between the equator and a pole
questions.why: The article discusses solar intensity in terms of how strong or concentrated the sun's heat energy is in a region.

wrong.B: Population is not what intensity refers to here.
wrong.C: Sky color is not discussed in the article.
wrong.D: Distance is a separate idea from intensity in the article.

questions.stem: Why does the dispersion of sunlight at the poles mean so little heat reaches the ground?
options: Because the poles are permanently shielded by the equator
Because sunlight somehow travels more slowly near the poles
Because the same amount of energy spreads over a wider area
Because invisible clouds block the light there
questions.why: In the article, at a low angle, sunlight spreads over a wider area, so each part of the ground receives less concentrated heat.

wrong.A: The equator does not shield the poles from sunlight.
wrong.B: The speed of sunlight is not discussed as a factor.
wrong.D: Invisible cloud-blocking is not mentioned as the cause.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why the equator can sustain more species than the poles?
options: The poles actually support more species than the equator
Its warm, humid, stable climate favors year-round growth
The equator technically has no climate, so anything can survive
Animals and plants generally prefer extreme cold over warmth
questions.why: The article links the equator's warm, humid, consistent climate to the thriving rainforests and diverse life found there, unlike the nearly lifeless poles.

wrong.A: The poles are described as supporting almost no vegetation.
wrong.C: The equator has a well-described, consistent climate.
wrong.D: The article links thriving life to warmth, not cold.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about human settlement patterns is best supported by the article?
options: More people actually live permanently at the poles than near the equator
Human settlement has no connection whatsoever to climate
The equator is uninhabited because of its extreme heat
Mild climate near the equator supports far larger populations than the poles
questions.why: The article contrasts the few people who live permanently at the poles, due to extreme ice and cold, with the many people supported by the equator's milder climate.

wrong.A: In the article, very few people live permanently at either pole.
wrong.B: The article directly connects climate to where people can live.
wrong.C: Many people are described as living near the equator.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly organized?
options: It presents a step-by-step guide for surviving polar cold, with a list of things to carry
It debates whether human-caused climate change is real, with arguments from each side
It narrates a fictional expedition toward the South Pole, with a hero and a dog
It defines the equator and poles, then traces their climate and the life each sustains
questions.why: The article moves from defining the equator and poles, to the cause of their differing sunlight intensity, to the resulting climate and life each sustains.

wrong.A: No survival guide is presented.
wrong.B: Climate change as a debate topic is not discussed.
wrong.C: No fictional expedition narrative is included.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why the equator and the poles represent opposite climate extremes, and how that climate affects what each region can sustain. Use the words intensity and sustain.
checklist: I explained why the equator and poles have opposite climates.
I explained what each region's climate allows it to sustain.
I used intensity and sustain correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The equator and the poles represent opposite climate extremes because of the intensity of sunlight each receives: the equator is struck almost perpendicularly by the sun nearly every day, while the poles receive sunlight at an extremely low, dispersed angle for most of the year. This difference in intensity means the equator's warm, humid climate can sustain dense rainforests and large human populations, while the poles' bitter cold, broken only by a brief summer thaw, can sustain almost no vegetation and only a small number of visiting scientists.

LOW.stem: How much heat do the poles get?
options: A lot of heat
Just a bit of heat
Heat from the woods
The same as the equator

wrong.A: The poles get only a little heat, not a lot.
wrong.C: The text does not say woods give heat to the poles.

wrong.D: The poles stay cold, not hot.

far
late

LOW.stem: Why might thick woods grow near the equator?

MID.stem: In the article, the word extreme most nearly means —

warmest
smallest
newest

What weather to expect there

hide
measure
support

HIGH.stem: Why is there little seasonal change at the equator?
